The statement signals a clear negative near‑term outlook from COVID‑19, but it also pairs that with aggressive easing—cutting the policy rate to the effective lower bound and launching large‑scale purchases of Treasuries and MBS—to stabilize aggregate demand and credit markets. Consistent with New Keynesian and credit‑channel evidence, such measures can lower external finance premia and dampen the real effects of adverse shocks, supporting the flow of credit to households and businesses. With market‑based inflation compensation declining and survey expectations little changed, the literature on inflation‑forecast targeting recommends forceful, transparent easing to keep expectations anchored around the symmetric 2 percent goal and reduce the risk of a liquidity‑trap/deflation dynamic. The use of discount window easing, ample repo operations, and coordinated dollar swap lines aligns with crisis‑era findings that central bank liquidity provision can prevent credit market dysfunction from amplifying real‑economy contractions. Overall tone remains negative due to expected near‑term contraction, but decisive policy actions modestly temper the downside.
